For years, much of the Israeli media told the public that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was corrupt and had to go. Today, the judges hearing his case suggested that prosecutors consider dropping the only case in which he was charged with bribery.

That is a stunning turn in a trial that helped tear Israel apart. In my view, what I call Israel’s deep state used the prosecution to put Netanyahu in the dock and relied on much of the media to convince the public he was already guilty. The campaign deepened the rift in Israeli society during a period of political paralysis in which we went to the polls five times in less than four years.

Here’s what the judges said today about each of the three cases.

Case 4000 - The bribery case. Prosecutors claimed that Netanyahu, while serving as communications minister, made decisions that benefited Bezeq, a major Israeli telecommunications company. In return, they alleged, a popular news website controlled by the same owner gave Netanyahu and his family favorable treatment. The judges said the chances of conviction were low. They also questioned the breach-of-trust charge and suggested that prosecutors consider dropping the entire case against him.

Case 2000 - The newspaper deal that never happened. Prosecutors alleged that Netanyahu discussed a deal with the publisher of a major Israeli newspaper. The publisher would give Netanyahu more favorable coverage, and Netanyahu would advance legislation to limit the circulation of a rival newspaper. The proposed deal never went ahead. Today, the judges expressed serious doubt that the conduct described by prosecutors even amounted to a crime.

Case 1000 - The gifts case. Prosecutors say Netanyahu and his family received cigars, champagne and other gifts from two wealthy businessmen, and that Netanyahu used his office to help one of them. Netanyahu says the gifts were given out of friendship. The judges left the outcome open and called for the case to be brought to a conclusion.

The court has yet to issue a verdict, but the judges signaled today that Netanyahu may be headed for acquittal in the bribery case, and that the newspaper case faces a serious question about whether there was a crime in the first place. These were the two cases that drove years of headlines.

Will the news outlets that spent years telling Israelis how strong the case was give today’s development the same airtime? Will they ask prosecutors why they brought a bribery charge that the judges are now suggesting they drop?

For years, they demanded answers from Netanyahu. After five elections and years of division, Israelis deserve answers from the prosecutors who brought these charges and the journalists who spent years treating them as a verdict.

U.S. Spy Agencies Hit by Cyber Breach, Raising Fresh Questions About Intelligence Security 🤖

A cybersecurity breach has struck parts of the U.S. intelligence community, exposing weaknesses in systems used by American spy agencies to collect and analyze publicly available information. 

The incident has drawn attention to the security of government networks, even those that do not handle classified intelligence.

The breach reportedly affected unclassified systems associated with the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI). 

These networks support intelligence work involving open-source information, including publicly accessible documents, online material and other data used to assess threats and monitor developments around the world.

Although the compromised systems were not classified, the incident is far from insignificant. Unclassified intelligence can still contain sensitive operational details, internal assessments and information that could help foreign adversaries better understand how U.S. intelligence agencies operate.

The breach also raises broader concerns about the growing sophistication of cyber threats targeting American government institutions. Intelligence agencies remain attractive targets for foreign hackers because even limited access can provide valuable insights into national security operations.

Officials have not publicly disclosed the full scope of the incident, including who may have been responsible or precisely what information was accessed. There is also no confirmed indication that classified intelligence was compromised.

The investigation is expected to focus on how the attackers gained access, how long they may have remained inside the affected systems and whether any information was extracted.

The incident highlights an uncomfortable reality for Washington: keeping classified intelligence secure is only part of the challenge. Protecting the vast network of unclassified systems that support America's intelligence operations is becoming equally critical.

As cyberattacks grow more sophisticated, even networks considered less sensitive can become valuable targets — and a potential weak point in U.S. national security.
